## {.center}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Part 1: What Is Light?
:::

*The electromagnetic wave*

---

## Light Is an Electromagnetic Wave {background-color="black"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
{{< fig electromagnetic-wave >}}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Electromagnetic wave:**

Self-propagating oscillation of electric and magnetic fields.

::: {.fragment}
Unlike sound or ocean waves — **no medium needed!**

Light travels perfectly through the vacuum of space.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
4–5 min. "This is why we can see starlight from billions of light-years away."
:::

---

## Two Key Properties {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

| Property | Symbol | What it measures | Units |
|----------|--------|------------------|-------|
| **Wavelength** | λ (lambda) | Distance between wave crests | meters (m) or nanometers (nm) |
| **Frequency** | f | Wave crests passing per second | hertz (Hz) |

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-center .text-xl}
All light travels at the same speed: $c = 3 \times 10^8$ m/s
:::

::: {.notes}
5–6 min. "Wavelength and frequency are the two key descriptors."
:::

---

## The Wave Equation {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl .bg-muted .p-3}
$$c = \lambda f$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
Since $c$ is constant:

- **Longer wavelength** ↔ **lower frequency**
- **Shorter wavelength** ↔ **higher frequency**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-muted}
Wavelength and frequency carry the same information — two ways to describe the same wave.
:::

::: {.notes}
6–7 min. "Double the wavelength means half the frequency."
:::

---

::: {.quiz}

- [ ] Twice the frequency
- [x] Half the frequency

:::

:::

## {.center}

::: {.r-fit-text}
The Electromagnetic Spectrum
:::

*More than meets the eye*

---

## Visible Light Is a Tiny Sliver {background-color="black"}

{{< fig jwst-em-spectrum >}}

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-center}
"Visible light" — the colors we see — is just a tiny fraction of the full spectrum.
:::

::: {.notes}
7–8 min. "Radio to gamma rays — all are light. All travel at speed c."
:::

---

## The Full Spectrum {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

| Region | Wavelength | Astronomical Uses |
|--------|------------|-------------------|
| **Radio** | > 10 cm | Mapping hydrogen, pulsars |
| **Microwave** | 1 mm – 10 cm | CMB, cold dust |
| **Infrared** | 700 nm – 1 mm | Dust-obscured regions, cool stars |
| **Visible** | 400 – 700 nm | Direct imaging, stellar classification |
| **Ultraviolet** | 10 – 400 nm | Hot gas, stellar nurseries |
| **X-ray** | 0.01 – 10 nm | Black holes, neutron stars |
| **Gamma ray** | < 0.01 nm | Supernovae, gamma-ray bursts |

::: {.notes}
8–9 min. "Different wavelengths reveal different physics."
:::

---

## Same Object, Different Wavelengths {background-color="black"}

{{< fig jwst-vs-hst-ngc1566 >}}

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-center}
**The universe looks different at every wavelength.**
:::

::: {.notes}
9–10 min. "This is why astronomers build different types of telescopes."
:::

---

- [ ] Microwave → Radio → Visible → Infrared → Gamma rays

## The Speed of Light {background-color="black"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl}
$c = 299,792,458$ m/s

~300,000 km/s
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
**This is the cosmic speed limit.**

Nothing with mass can reach it.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-muted}
And because light has finite speed...

**looking out in space is looking back in time.**
:::

::: {.notes}
10–11 min. "The farther we see, the younger the universe appears."
:::

---

## Light-Travel Time {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

| Object | Distance | Light-Travel Time |
|--------|----------|-------------------|
| Moon | 384,000 km | 1.3 seconds |
| Sun | 150 million km | 8 minutes |
| Proxima Centauri | 4.2 light-years | 4.2 years |
| Andromeda Galaxy | 2.5 million light-years | 2.5 million years |
| Distant galaxies | Billions of light-years | Billions of years |

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-muted}
When we observe the most distant galaxies, we're seeing the early universe directly.
:::

::: {.notes}
11–12 min. "The farther we look, the farther back in time we see."
:::

---

## {.center}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Part 2: Why Is the Sky Blue?
:::

*Rayleigh scattering*

---

## Sunlight Is All Colors {background-color="black"}

{{< fig prism-spectrum-jwst >}}

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
Sunlight is **white light** — a mix of all visible wavelengths.

So why does the sky favor blue?
:::

::: {.notes}
12–13 min. "If sunlight has all colors, why is the sky blue?"
:::

---

## Rayleigh Scattering {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl .bg-muted .p-3}
$$\text{Scattering} \propto \frac{1}{\lambda^4}$$

**Shorter wavelengths scatter MUCH more.**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
Comparing blue ($\lambda \approx 450$ nm) and red ($\lambda \approx 700$ nm):

$$\left(\frac{700}{450}\right)^4 \approx 6$$

Blue scatters about **6× more** than red!
:::

::: {.notes}
13–14 min. "The 1/λ⁴ makes a huge difference."
:::

---

## Why the Sky Is Blue {background-color="black"}

{{< fig rayleigh-scattering-sky >}}

::: {.fragment}
Blue photons scatter all over the sky → reach your eyes from every direction.

Red photons mostly travel straight through.
:::

::: {.notes}
14–15 min. "Blue gets scattered everywhere; red goes straight through."
:::

---

## Why Sunsets Are Red {background-color="black"}

{{< fig sunset-scattering >}}

::: {.fragment}
At sunset, sunlight travels through **much more atmosphere**.

Blue is scattered away → you see the remaining **reds and oranges**.
:::

::: {.notes}
15–16 min. "Same physics, different geometry."
:::

---

:::

::: {.notes}
1 min. iClicker poll.
:::

During a total lunar eclipse, the Moon doesn't go dark — it turns **deep red**.

## Earth's Atmosphere as Filter {background-color="black"}

{{< fig lunar-eclipse-red >}}

::: {.fragment}
1. Sunlight passes through Earth's atmosphere
2. Blue light scatters away (Rayleigh!)
3. Only **red light** makes it through
4. That red light bends toward the Moon
:::

::: {.notes}
17–18 min. "It's the light from every sunset on Earth, focused on the Moon."
:::

## Inverse-Square Law for Light {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.text-center .text-xl .bg-muted .p-3}
$$I \propto \frac{1}{r^2}$$

**Double your distance → receive 1/4 the intensity**
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
Why? Light spreads over spheres.

Sphere area $= 4\pi r^2$ → intensity drops as $1/r^2$.
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-muted}
Same geometric argument as gravity (L6)!
:::

::: {.notes}
18–19 min. "Same spreading-over-spheres argument as gravity."
:::

---

## {background-color="black"}

{{< fig light-inverse-square >}}

::: {.notes}
19–20 min. Visual of inverse-square spreading.
:::

---

## Distance and Brightness {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

| Distance Change | Intensity Change |
|-----------------|------------------|
| 2× farther | 1/4 as bright |
| 3× farther | 1/9 as bright |
| 10× farther | 1/100 as bright |
| 100× farther | 1/10,000 as bright |

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .text-center}
**If we know true luminosity and measure apparent brightness, we can calculate distance!**
:::

::: {.notes}
20–21 min. "This is the foundation of distance measurement in astronomy."
:::

---

## Quick Check: Distance and Brightness {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
A star appears 16 times fainter than an identical star nearby. How much farther away is the faint star?

- [x] 4× farther
- [ ] 16× farther
- [ ] 8× farther
- [ ] 2× farther
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-sm}
**Solution:** $I \propto 1/r^2$. If $I = 1/16$, then $r = 4$.
:::

::: {.notes}
1–2 min. iClicker poll, then explain.
:::

---

## Quick Check: Two Stars {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
Star A is 5× farther away than Star B. If they have the same luminosity, Star A appears:

- [ ] 5× fainter
- [ ] 10× fainter
- [x] 25× fainter
- [ ] 125× fainter
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-sm}
**Solution:** Distance ×5 → intensity drops by $5^2 = 25$.
:::

::: {.notes}
1–2 min. iClicker poll, then explain.
:::

## Key Takeaways {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.text-sm}

1. **Light is an electromagnetic wave.** $c = \lambda f$ where $c = 3 \times 10^8$ m/s.

2. **The EM spectrum spans radio → gamma rays.** Visible light is a tiny sliver.

3. **Rayleigh scattering:** Short wavelengths scatter more ($\propto 1/\lambda^4$). Sky = blue. Sunset = red.

4. **Lunar eclipses are red** — same physics as sunsets, projected on the Moon.

5. **Light intensity follows the inverse-square law:** $I \propto 1/r^2$.

6. **Light is the astronomer's primary tool.** We extract temperature, composition, motion, and distance — all from light.

:::

::: {.notes}
21–23 min. Rapid recap.
:::

## {.center background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Numerical Verification
:::

*Checking the wave equation and scattering*

::: {.notes}
Let's verify our equations with explicit calculations.
:::

---

## Verifying c = λf {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Given:** Red light has wavelength $\lambda = 700$ nm. What's its frequency?

::: {.fragment}
**Step 1: Convert wavelength to meters**

$$\lambda = 700 \text{ nm} \times \frac{10^{-9} \text{ m}}{1 \text{ nm}} = 7.00 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Step 2: Solve for frequency**

$$f = \frac{c}{\lambda} = \frac{3.00 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}}{7.00 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$f = 4.29 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz} = 4.29 \times 10^{14} \text{ s}^{-1}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2 .text-muted}
**Unit check:** $\frac{\text{m/s}}{\text{m}} = \frac{1}{\text{s}} = \text{Hz}$ ✓
:::

::: {.notes}
"Red light oscillates 429 trillion times per second. That's what frequency means."
:::

---

## Frequency Comparison Across the Spectrum {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

| Type | Wavelength | Frequency | Calculation |
|------|------------|-----------|-------------|
| Radio (FM) | 3 m | $10^8$ Hz | $\frac{3 \times 10^8}{3} = 10^8$ |
| Microwave | 1 cm | $3 \times 10^{10}$ Hz | $\frac{3 \times 10^8}{10^{-2}}$ |
| Red light | 700 nm | $4.3 \times 10^{14}$ Hz | $\frac{3 \times 10^8}{7 \times 10^{-7}}$ |
| Blue light | 450 nm | $6.7 \times 10^{14}$ Hz | $\frac{3 \times 10^8}{4.5 \times 10^{-7}}$ |
| X-ray | 1 nm | $3 \times 10^{17}$ Hz | $\frac{3 \times 10^8}{10^{-9}}$ |

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
**Pattern:** Shorter wavelength → higher frequency (always!)
:::

::: {.notes}
"The relationship is inverse. As λ decreases, f increases proportionally."
:::

---

## Rayleigh Scattering: Full Calculation {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**How much more does blue scatter than red?**

Blue: $\lambda_b = 450$ nm, Red: $\lambda_r = 700$ nm

::: {.fragment}
**Scattering ratio:**

$$\frac{\text{Scattering}_{\text{blue}}}{\text{Scattering}_{\text{red}}} = \frac{1/\lambda_b^4}{1/\lambda_r^4} = \left(\frac{\lambda_r}{\lambda_b}\right)^4$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$= \left(\frac{700 \text{ nm}}{450 \text{ nm}}\right)^4 = (1.556)^4$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$= 5.86 \approx 6$$
:::

::: {.fragment .bg-muted .p-2}
**Blue light scatters ~6× more than red light.**

Units cancel (nm/nm)⁴ = dimensionless ratio ✓
:::

::: {.notes}
"The fourth power makes a huge difference. Even a modest wavelength ratio becomes significant."
:::

---

## Why Not Violet? {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

Violet ($\lambda \approx 400$ nm) scatters even MORE than blue:

$$\left(\frac{700}{400}\right)^4 = (1.75)^4 = 9.4$$

**Violet scatters 9× more than red!**

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
**So why isn't the sky violet?**

1. The Sun emits **less violet** than blue (blackbody spectrum)
2. Our eyes are **less sensitive** to violet
3. Some violet is absorbed by ozone
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
**Result:** We perceive the scattered light as **blue**, not violet.
:::

::: {.notes}
"Physics says violet should dominate, but the Sun's spectrum and our eye sensitivity favor blue."
:::

---

## Inverse-Square Law: Star Distance Problem {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Problem:** Star A appears 100× fainter than Star B. If they're identical, how much farther is Star A?

::: {.fragment}
**From inverse-square law:**

$$\frac{I_A}{I_B} = \frac{r_B^2}{r_A^2}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$\frac{1}{100} = \frac{r_B^2}{r_A^2}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Solving for distance ratio:**

$$\frac{r_A}{r_B} = \sqrt{100} = 10$$
:::

::: {.fragment .bg-success-subtle .p-2}
**Star A is 10× farther away.**

Note: We don't need absolute distances — just the ratio!
:::

::: {.notes}
"This is how astronomers bootstrap the distance ladder. Compare identical objects at different distances."
:::

---

## Light Travel Time: Proxima Centauri {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Given:** Proxima Centauri is 4.24 light-years away. Express this in km.

::: {.fragment}
**Step 1: How far does light travel in 1 year?**

$$d_{1\text{yr}} = c \times t = (3.00 \times 10^5 \text{ km/s}) \times (1 \text{ year})$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Convert 1 year to seconds:**

$$1 \text{ yr} = 365.25 \text{ days} \times 24 \text{ hr/day} \times 3600 \text{ s/hr} = 3.156 \times 10^7 \text{ s}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$d_{1\text{ly}} = 3.00 \times 10^5 \times 3.156 \times 10^7 = 9.47 \times 10^{12} \text{ km}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Distance to Proxima Centauri:**

$$d = 4.24 \times 9.47 \times 10^{12} \text{ km} = 4.01 \times 10^{13} \text{ km}$$
:::

::: {.notes}
"40 trillion km to the nearest star. Space is incomprehensibly vast."
:::

---

## {.center background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Deeper Dive
:::

*Photon energy and the quantum nature of light*

::: {.notes}
Optional advanced content bridging to L8-L9.
:::

---

## Light as Particles: Photons {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

Light behaves as both a **wave** and a **particle**.

Each particle of light — a **photon** — carries energy:

$$E = hf = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$$

::: {.fragment}
**Where:**

- $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}$ J·s (Planck's constant)
- $c = 3.00 \times 10^8$ m/s
- $hc = 1.986 \times 10^{-25}$ J·m
:::

::: {.notes}
"This quantum nature of light is what we'll need to understand spectral lines in L9."
:::

---

## Photon Energy: Useful Forms {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

**In Joules** (SI units):

$$E = \frac{1.986 \times 10^{-25} \text{ J·m}}{\lambda \text{ (in meters)}}$$

::: {.fragment}
**In electron-volts** (more convenient for atoms):

$$E = \frac{1240 \text{ eV·nm}}{\lambda \text{ (in nm)}}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4}
**Example:** Red photon ($\lambda = 620$ nm)

$$E = \frac{1240 \text{ eV·nm}}{620 \text{ nm}} = 2.0 \text{ eV}$$
:::

::: {.notes}
"The 1240 eV·nm is a convenient number to memorize. It comes from hc in these units."
:::

---

## Where Does 1240 eV·nm Come From? {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

::: {.text-sm}
$$hc = (6.626 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J·s}) \times (3.00 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s})$$

$$= 1.988 \times 10^{-25} \text{ J·m}$$

::: {.fragment}
**Convert J to eV:**

$$1 \text{ eV} = 1.602 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$$

$$hc = \frac{1.988 \times 10^{-25} \text{ J·m}}{1.602 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J/eV}} = 1.241 \times 10^{-6} \text{ eV·m}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Convert m to nm:**

$$hc = 1.241 \times 10^{-6} \text{ eV·m} \times \frac{10^9 \text{ nm}}{1 \text{ m}} = 1241 \text{ eV·nm}$$
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .bg-muted .p-2}
We round to **1240 eV·nm** for convenience.
:::

::: {.notes}
"I'm showing you the derivation so you understand where this number comes from. Always know your units!"
:::

---

## Photon Energies Across the Spectrum {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

| Light Type | Wavelength | Energy | Calculation |
|------------|------------|--------|-------------|
| Radio | 1 m = 10⁹ nm | $1.24 \times 10^{-6}$ eV | $\frac{1240}{10^9}$ |
| Infrared | 10,000 nm | 0.124 eV | $\frac{1240}{10000}$ |
| Red | 620 nm | 2.0 eV | $\frac{1240}{620}$ |
| Blue | 450 nm | 2.76 eV | $\frac{1240}{450}$ |
| UV | 100 nm | 12.4 eV | $\frac{1240}{100}$ |
| X-ray | 1 nm | 1,240 eV | $\frac{1240}{1}$ |

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
**Pattern:** Shorter wavelength = higher energy photons
:::

::: {.notes}
"This is why X-rays are dangerous and radio waves aren't. It's about energy per photon."
:::

---

## Why UV Causes Sunburn {background-color="#0a2f5c"}

**Key threshold:** Breaking chemical bonds requires ~3-10 eV.

::: {.fragment}
- **Visible light** (1.8-3.1 eV): Not enough energy to break bonds
- **UV-A** (3.1-3.9 eV): Can damage some molecules
- **UV-B** (3.9-4.4 eV): Breaks DNA bonds → sunburn
- **UV-C** (4.4-12.4 eV): Very damaging (blocked by ozone)
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-4 .bg-warning-subtle .p-2}
**It's not about intensity — it's about energy per photon.**

A trillion low-energy photons won't break a bond that one high-energy photon can.
:::

::: {.notes}
"This is why you can sit under a bright red lamp all day with no damage, but minutes of UV causes burns."
:::
